TB is an infection mainly of the lung tissue; it can spread to meninges, kidneys, bones and lymph nodes. The organism, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, is an acid-fast aerobic rod, slow-growing, sensitive to heat and ultraviolet light, and spread person to person by AIRBORNE transmission.

## Findings
- Fatigue, loss of appetite, weight loss, low-grade fever, night sweats.
- Cough starting slowly, becoming more frequent with mucoid or pus-like sputum.
- Hemoptysis, chest pain and dyspnea suggest extensive disease.

## Diagnosis
- Sputum smear and culture confirm TB.
- Chest X-ray shows extent.
- Tuberculin skin test (PPD/Mantoux) shows exposure, not necessarily active disease.

## Classification (handout)
- Class 0: no exposure, no infection.
- Class 1: exposure, no infection evidence.
- Class 2: latent infection, no disease (positive PPD).
- Class 3: active disease.
- Class 4: disease, not clinically active.
- Class 5: suspected, diagnosis pending.

## Nursing priority
Airborne precautions: negative-pressure room and a particulate (N95-type) respirator for staff, mask for the client during transport.

## How the exam asks about it
- Which test confirms (sputum); which precautions (airborne); what a positive PPD means.

## Related topics
[[Anti-TB Drugs and Nursing Care]], [[Expanded Program on Immunization]], [[BCG and Pentavalent Vaccine]], [[Occupational Lung Diseases: Asbestosis, Silicosis, Sarcoidosis]]

## Check against your textbook
- Airborne precaution details are added from standard textbooks. Philippine TB programs use their own case definitions; the class system here is the older American one.

title: Anti-TB Drugs and Nursing Care
body:
## What it is
Pulmonary TB is treated with several drugs together for a long time (handout: 6 to 12 months).

## Regimen from the handout
- Initial phase: isoniazid (INH), rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol daily for 8 weeks.
- Continuation phase: INH and rifampin for another 4 or 7 months.
- Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) is given with INH to prevent peripheral neuropathy.

## Main side effects
- INH: peripheral neuritis, raised liver enzymes, hepatitis, hypersensitivity.
- Rifampin: hepatitis, fever, nausea and vomiting; (orange-colored body fluids is standard teaching).
- Pyrazinamide: high uric acid, liver toxicity, rash, joint pain, GI upset.
- Ethambutol: optic neuritis (vision changes, color discrimination), rash.
- Handout doses: INH 5 mg/kg (max 300 mg); rifampin 10 mg/kg (max 600 mg); pyrazinamide 15 to 30 mg/kg (max 2 g); ethambutol 15 to 25 mg/kg.

## Nursing actions
- Take on an empty stomach or at least 1 hour before meals (food reduces absorption).
- Avoid tyramine- and histamine-rich foods with INH (headache, flushing, low BP, palpitations, sweating).
- Monitor for side effects, especially liver and vision.
- Stress completing the whole regimen: stopping early causes drug-resistant TB.
- Hygiene: cover the mouth when coughing, dispose of tissues, wash hands.
- Rest, fluids, small frequent nutritious meals.

## How the exam asks about it
- Match drug to adverse effect; what to teach about adherence.

## Related topics
[[Pulmonary Tuberculosis: Diagnosis and Classification]], [[Essential Drugs]], [[Treatment of CD, NCD and Emergency Services]]

## Check against your textbook
- Doses, the 8-week/4-7 month schedule and the food advice are from the handout and may differ from the DOH program. Verify before relying on them. Rifampin sometimes taken with food in practice if GI upset.

title: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)
body:
## What it is
A severe form of acute lung injury: sudden, progressive pulmonary edema with bilateral infiltrates on chest X-ray and hypoxemia that does not improve with oxygen, without raised left atrial pressure. Lung compliance falls.

## Findings
- Develops over about 4 to 48 hours.
- Severe dyspnea, labored fast breathing, severe hypoxemia unresponsive to oxygen.
- Crackles and rhonchi, increased alveolar dead space.
- X-ray looks like cardiogenic pulmonary edema.

## Diagnostics
History and presentation, ABG showing hypoxemia despite more oxygen, bilateral infiltrates, BNP and echocardiogram (to exclude heart failure), pulmonary artery catheter.

## Treatment
- Treat the cause; optimise oxygenation.
- Intubation and mechanical ventilation with PEEP, sedation, sometimes paralytics, antibiotics as indicated.
- Supportive: surfactant replacement and other drugs mentioned in the handout.

## Priority nursing actions
1. ICU monitoring, frequent reassessment.
2. Turn the client often to improve ventilation, perfusion and drainage.
3. Promote rest to cut oxygen demand.
4. Nutrition: 35 to 45 kcal/kg/day (handout).
5. Reassure; look for anxiety linked to ventilator problems.

## How the exam asks about it
- Hypoxemia not corrected by oxygen with bilateral white-out. See also [[Respiratory Failure Recognition]].

## Related topics
[[Pneumonia]], [[Sepsis and Septic Shock Recognition]], [[Pulmonary Embolism]]

## Check against your textbook
- Surfactant and "pulmonary antihypertensive" drugs are not standard in all references; verify.

title: Pulmonary Embolism
body:
## What it is
Blockage of the pulmonary artery or a branch by a clot, usually from a deep vein (see [[Deep Vein Thrombosis]]). Risks: trauma, surgery (orthopedic, abdominal, pelvic), pregnancy, heart failure, age over 50, clotting disorders, immobility.

## Findings
- Dyspnea (most common symptom) and tachypnea (most frequent sign).
- Sudden pleuritic chest pain that can mimic angina or MI.
- Anxiety, tachycardia, fever, cough, sweating, hemoptysis, syncope, petechiae over the chest.

## Diagnostics
- Pulmonary angiography (best method per the handout), V/Q scan, spiral CT.
- ABG: low oxygen and low CO2. ECG: sinus tachycardia, nonspecific T changes. Chest X-ray: infiltrates, atelectasis, raised diaphragm.

## Treatment
- Oxygen immediately, IV access, dobutamine or dopamine for hypotension, small doses of IV morphine for anxiety and chest pain.
- Anticoagulants (heparin, warfarin); thrombolytics (urokinase, streptokinase, alteplase) in severe cases; embolectomy for massive PE.

## Priority nursing actions (ABC)
1. Oxygen, raise the head of the bed, call the provider.
2. Monitor hypoxia, bleeding from anticoagulants, and signs of right ventricular failure or cardiogenic shock.
3. Prevent recurrence: early ambulation, leg exercises, avoid crossing legs, constrictive clothing and long sitting or bed rest.

## How the exam asks about it
- Sudden dyspnea and chest pain after surgery or long immobility. Compare with [[Myocardial Infarction: Presentation and Cardiac Markers]] and [[Angina Pectoris: Types, Triggers and Findings]].

## Related topics
[[Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)]], [[Respiratory Failure Recognition]], [[Cardiac Arrest and Basic Life Support Principles]]

title: Nitroglycerin: Forms, Action and Safe Use
body:
## What it is
Nitroglycerin is the classic nitrate for angina. It dilates the veins, so blood pools in the body's veins and less blood returns to the heart. That lowers preload and the heart's workload and oxygen demand. It also widens coronary arteries and lowers afterload to some degree.

## Must-know facts
- Forms named in the handout: sublingual tablet, spray, topical (ointment), and intravenous.
- Brand names listed: Nitrostat, Nitro-Bid.
- In angina, the aim is short-term and long-term cutting of myocardial oxygen use by vasodilation.
- In heart failure, nitroglycerin ointment or nitroprusside is used as a vasodilator to reduce preload and ease dyspnea.
- In MI, nitroglycerin is part of the standard drug set (the MONA idea: morphine, oxygen, nitroglycerin, aspirin).

## Assessment
- Before each dose: chest pain description, blood pressure and heart rate.
- After: is the pain gone? Is the client dizzy or hypotensive?

## Priority nursing actions
1. Stop activity and have the client sit or rest: rest alone reduces oxygen demand and sitting guards against a fall if pressure drops (safety).
2. Check blood pressure before giving it; vasodilation can drop pressure, so do not give if the pressure is dangerously low (follow the order).
3. Give the form ordered. For a tablet under the tongue, let it dissolve; do not swallow it.
4. Reassess pain and pressure. Pain that is not relieved, or is lasting or worsening, is treated as possible MI: call for help, get an ECG (the exam wants action, not waiting).

## Complications and red flags
- Hypotension, dizziness, headache and flushing are common effects of vasodilation.
- Pain not relieved by rest and nitroglycerin suggests unstable angina or MI.

## Client teaching
- Keep the medicine with you; use it at the first sign of an attack as prescribed.
- Rise slowly, because pressure may fall.
- Report chest pain that is not relieved, so the care team can act.
- Do not stop the regular medicines or change the schedule without the prescriber.

## How the exam asks about it
- Why does nitroglycerin help angina? Fewer veins returning blood = less preload = less oxygen demand.
- Stable angina eases with rest or nitroglycerin; pain that does not ease raises the alarm.

## Related topics
[[Angina Treatment: Procedures and Drugs]], [[Angina Pectoris: Types, Triggers and Findings]], [[Myocardial Infarction: Management and Drug Therapy]], [[Drugs Used in Heart Failure]]

## Check against your textbook
- Exact number of doses, spacing and storage rules, and interactions (for example with erectile-dysfunction drugs) are not in the handout. Confirm them in your drug book.

title: Antiplatelet and Anticoagulant Drugs in Cardiac Care
body:
## What it is
Two different jobs. Antiplatelets stop platelets sticking together (arterial clots, as in angina and MI). Anticoagulants slow the clotting cascade so a thrombus does not form or grow (as in venous clots, atrial thrombus, PE). Thrombolytics (clot busters) are a third group that dissolves a clot that already exists.

## Must-know facts
- Antiplatelets in the handout: aspirin; clopidogrel (Plavix); glycoprotein agents abciximab (ReoPro), tirofiban (Aggrastat), eptifibatide (Integrilin). Prasugrel is also named under the "thienopyridines".
- Anticoagulants in the handout: heparin (unfractionated); low-molecular-weight heparins enoxaparin (Lovenox) and dalteparin (Fragmin); warfarin (Coumadin) by mouth.
- Thrombolytics in the handout: alteplase (Activase, t-PA), urokinase, streptokinase.
- Monitoring in the handout: aPTT, prothrombin time (PT) and INR for the anticoagulated client.
- Mitral stenosis: anticoagulants may be used to lower the risk of atrial thrombus.
- DVT: subcutaneous heparin or LMWH is used in prevention for surgical clients; warfarin is the oral drug.

## Assessment
- Bleeding signs: bruising, gum or nose bleeding, blood in urine, stool or vomit, falling BP with rising pulse.
- Lab trends: aPTT, PT/INR as ordered; platelet count.
- Neurologic checks if headache or confusion appears (possible bleeding).

## Priority nursing actions
1. Check the right lab before each dose, because dose depends on the result (safety).
2. Watch for bleeding at every contact; report promptly.
3. Use soft techniques: soft toothbrush, electric razor, gentle handling, pressure on puncture sites.
4. Give subcutaneous injections as ordered without rubbing the site (general practice; check your fundamentals book).
5. Keep the antidote and emergency measures known to the unit.

## Treatment and medications
- Antiplatelet aim: prevent platelet aggregation, so artery stents and plaques do not clot.
- Heparin/LMWH: prevent thrombus formation or extension of an existing one.
- Warfarin: long-term oral control; the dose is guided by blood tests.

## Complications and red flags
- Bleeding is the main danger of every drug in this group. Sudden severe headache, black stools, or a falling BP means act at once.

## Client teaching
- Report bleeding or black stools; avoid unnecessary falls and injuries.
- Take at the same time daily; do not skip or double.
- Keep appointments for blood tests.
- Tell every provider and dentist what you take.

## How the exam asks about it
- Which lab monitors warfarin (PT/INR) versus heparin (aPTT)? Which group works on arterial clots (antiplatelets) versus venous clots (anticoagulants)?

## Related topics
[[Anticoagulants: Heparin and Warfarin]], [[Thrombolytic Drugs]], [[Deep Vein Thrombosis]], [[Myocardial Infarction: Management and Drug Therapy]], [[Angina Treatment: Procedures and Drugs]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout does not say which lab goes with which drug; the pairing of aPTT with heparin and PT/INR with warfarin is standard teaching: verify. Antidotes, diet rules for warfarin and dosing are not in the handout.

title: Chest Pain Compared: Angina, MI, Pericarditis, Pulmonary Embolism, Pleurisy
body:
## What it is
Many conditions hurt in the chest. The exam gives you a short description and expects you to sort it by what makes the pain better or worse, how long it lasts, and what else is present.

## Must-know facts
- Stable angina: pressure or heaviness behind the sternum, brought on by exertion, cold, a heavy meal or stress; eased by rest or nitroglycerin; short.
- Unstable angina: more frequent, more severe, may not ease with rest or nitroglycerin.
- Prinzmetal (variant) angina: pain at rest, ST elevation that reverses, thought to be coronary spasm.
- Myocardial infarction: pain usually longer than 30 minutes, spreads to the left arm, back or jaw, often starts without a cause (often morning), relieved only by opioids; with nausea, sweating, fear, shortness of breath.
- Pericarditis: pain under the clavicle, in the neck or left scapula; worse on deep inspiration, eased by sitting and leaning forward; friction rub.
- Pleurisy: sharp, knife-like pain on inspiration, cough or sneeze; limited to one area; pleural friction rub; eased by lying on the painful side.
- Pulmonary embolism: sudden pleuritic pain, may mimic angina or MI; dyspnea and tachypnea are the most frequent signs.
- Pneumonia: pleuritic pain with fever and productive cough.
- Pneumothorax: sudden chest discomfort with dyspnea, hyperresonance and diminished breath sounds.

## Assessment
- PQRST of pain: provoking factors, quality, radiation, severity, time.
- Vital signs, oxygen saturation, breath sounds, heart sounds (rub, S3, S4, muffled).
- ECG for any chest pain with a cardiac look.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Airway, breathing, circulation: oxygen, monitor, vital signs (ABC).
2. Get an ECG and notify the provider for chest pain that may be cardiac: the exam rewards early action over long assessment when MI is possible.
3. Give ordered drugs (nitroglycerin, aspirin, opioid) in the order given by the protocol.
4. Keep the client at rest and calm: anxiety raises oxygen demand.

## Complications and red flags
- Pain with falling BP, sweating and dysrhythmia suggests MI or shock.
- Pain with muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins and low BP suggests tamponade.
- Sudden dyspnea with tracheal shift suggests tension pneumothorax.

## How the exam asks about it
- Matching clue to disease: leaning forward eases = pericarditis; pain worse with breathing and rub = pleurisy; not relieved by rest or nitroglycerin and lasts over 30 minutes = MI.

## How to reason about it
Cause, finding, action: if you cannot rule out the heart, treat it as the heart. Oxygen and ECG come before comfort measures.

## Related topics
[[Angina Pectoris: Types, Triggers and Findings]], [[Myocardial Infarction: Presentation and Cardiac Markers]], [[Pericarditis and Pericardiocentesis]], [[Pleurisy (Pleuritis)]], [[Pulmonary Embolism]]

title: ECG Changes Linked to Cardiac and Electrolyte Disorders
body:
## What it is
A collection of the ECG clues the handout ties to specific disorders. Know the normal values first, then the changes.

## Must-know facts
- P wave: atrial depolarization; no wider than 0.12 second.
- PR interval: 0.12 to 0.20 second (conduction through atria, AV junction, Purkinje system).
- QRS: ventricular depolarization; 0.04 to 0.10 second.
- T wave: ventricular repolarization; over 5 mm is not normal.
- QT interval: usually 0.32 to 0.40; prolonged QT raises risk of torsades de pointes, a lethal ventricular dysrhythmia.
- U wave: usually unseen; may appear with hypokalemia.
- Disease-linked changes:
  - Angina (ischemia): T-wave inversion, ST depression.
  - Prinzmetal angina: reversible ST elevation at rest.
  - MI: T-wave changes, ST elevation, abnormal Q wave.
  - Myocarditis: low-voltage QRS, ST elevation or heart block.
  - Pulmonary embolism: sinus tachycardia, PR-interval depression, non-specific T-wave changes.
  - Restrictive cardiomyopathy: heart block can occur.
  - Mitral stenosis: atrial dysrhythmias.
- Rate: PP interval gives atrial rate; RR interval gives ventricular rate.

## Assessment
- Read rate, rhythm, then intervals. Any new change in a client with chest pain is reported.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Treat the client, not the monitor: check pulse, BP, color and symptoms first (assess before intervening).
2. For a dangerous rhythm or new ST change, call for help and keep emergency equipment ready.
3. Check serum potassium and other electrolytes when the pattern suggests it, per orders.

## Complications and red flags
- Prolonged QT or runs of wide complexes, new Q waves, heart block.

## How the exam asks about it
- Match change to condition: U wave = low potassium; ST elevation = MI or variant angina; T inversion and ST depression = ischemia.

## How to reason about it
ST depression = ischemia that is reversible; ST elevation with abnormal Q = tissue damage or spasm. The exam usually wants you to act on the client first.

## Related topics
[[ECG Waves and Intervals]], [[Angina Pectoris: Types, Triggers and Findings]], [[Myocardial Infarction: Presentation and Cardiac Markers]], [[Myocarditis]], [[Pulmonary Embolism]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout states the T wave limit as "not normal more than 5 mm" and the AV node delay as "0.8 milliseconds"; both look garbled. Confirm normal values in your textbook.

title: Valve Lesions and Murmurs Compared
body:
## What it is
Four valve problems share a family of exam questions. Learn each by three things: what part of the heart cycle is affected, the sound, and the main symptom.

## Must-know facts
- Mitral stenosis: narrowed mitral valve; usually rheumatic. Low-pitched rumbling diastolic murmur at the apex. Blood backs up into the left atrium then lungs: dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, hemoptysis, atrial dysrhythmias; right heart failure late.
- Mitral regurgitation: leaky mitral valve; blood flows back into left atrium in systole. High-pitched blowing systolic murmur at the apex. Common causes: mitral valve prolapse and rheumatic heart disease. Fatigue, weakness, palpitations, dyspnea, cough.
- Mitral valve prolapse: leaflets bulge into the left atrium in systole.
- Aortic stenosis: narrowed aortic valve; loud rough systolic murmur over the aortic area; the left ventricle thickens. Classic triad: exertional dyspnea, angina, syncope or dizziness. BP is normal.
- Aortic regurgitation: blood flows back into the left ventricle in diastole. High-pitched blowing diastolic murmur at the left sternal border, 3rd to 4th intercostal space. Widened pulse pressure, water-hammer (Corrigan's) pulse, visible pulsations in neck and head.

## Assessment
- Auscultate at the correct site and phase; note pulse pressure, rhythm, weight, edema, lung sounds.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Breathing first: high Fowler's position for dyspnea (mitral stenosis).
2. Watch for pulmonary edema, thrombus and dysrhythmias; check ABG as ordered.
3. Daily weight for fluid balance; low-sodium diet teaching.
4. Reduce exertion in aortic regurgitation; vasodilators and ACE inhibitors may be ordered.

## Treatment and medications
- Mitral stenosis: anticoagulants against atrial clot; valvuloplasty or valve replacement.
- Mitral regurgitation: afterload reduction with ACE inhibitors; valve repair or replacement.
- Aortic regurgitation: valvuloplasty or replacement, ideally before left ventricular failure; vasodilators.
- Aortic stenosis: valve replacement or percutaneous valvuloplasty.

## Complications and red flags
- Pulmonary edema, heart failure, atrial clots, syncope, infective endocarditis risk.

## How the exam asks about it
- "Rumbling diastolic at the apex" = mitral stenosis. "Blowing systolic at the apex" = mitral regurgitation. "Rough systolic at the aortic area with syncope" = aortic stenosis. "Water-hammer pulse, wide pulse pressure" = aortic regurgitation.

## Memory aid
Stenosis = a stiff, narrow door: sound occurs when blood must pass through (mitral stenosis in diastole when the ventricle fills; aortic stenosis in systole when it empties). Regurgitation = leak: sound when the valve should be closed.

## Related topics
[[Valvular Heart Disease: Overview and Mitral Stenosis]], [[Mitral Regurgitation and Mitral Valve Prolapse]], [[Aortic Stenosis]], [[Aortic Regurgitation]], [[Heart Sounds S1 to S4]]

title: Acute Pulmonary Edema
body:
## What it is
Fluid floods the lung tissue and alveoli, usually because the left heart cannot move blood forward. Pressure backs up into the pulmonary veins and fluid is forced out of the capillaries. Gas exchange fails.

## Must-know facts
- Main cause in the handout: left-sided heart failure. Also a complication of mitral stenosis, aortic stenosis, and of surgery on a stenosed mitral valve.
- ARDS also has pulmonary edema but is a lung injury problem with normal left atrial pressure.
- Hallmark sign: frothy, pink (blood-tinged) sputum.
- Other findings: severe dyspnea, orthopnea, cough, crackles, low oxygen saturation, anxiety, S3 gallop.

## Assessment
- Rate and effort of breathing, oxygen saturation, breath sounds, sputum, BP and pulse, mental state.
- Daily weight, intake and output, edema.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Sit the client upright (high Fowler's or semi-Fowler's), legs dependent if ordered: gravity pools blood in the legs and eases breathing (airway and breathing first).
2. Give oxygen as ordered to treat hypoxemia and reduce heart workload.
3. Give diuretics as ordered to pull fluid off; watch potassium.
4. Give other ordered vasodilators and cardiac drugs; opioid for anxiety and chest tightness per order.
5. Stay with the client; fear worsens workload.
6. Record intake and output and monitor response.

## Treatment and medications
- Diuretics (furosemide and others), vasodilators (nitroglycerin, nitroprusside), inotropes (digoxin, dobutamine), ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers for long-term HF control.

## Complications and red flags
- Respiratory failure, shock, dysrhythmias, pneumonia.

## Client teaching
- Low-sodium diet; weigh daily and report quick gain; take heart failure drugs as prescribed; sleep with head raised.

## How the exam asks about it
- Pink frothy sputum plus crackles in HF = pulmonary edema. First action: upright position and oxygen, then drugs.

## How to reason about it
Cause (weak left ventricle) -> finding (fluid in lungs, froth) -> action (sit up, oxygen, diuretic). Trap: lying the client flat for comfort or for an exam.

## Related topics
[[Left-Sided versus Right-Sided Heart Failure]], [[Drugs Used in Heart Failure]], [[Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)]], [[Diuretics: Thiazide, Loop, Osmotic and Potassium-Sparing]]

## Check against your textbook
- Dependent leg positioning and the opioid role are standard teaching rather than handout text: verify.

title: Common Cold (Viral Rhinitis)
body:
## What it is
The most frequent viral infection in the general population. The handout names coronavirus as the cause. The virus spreads easily because it is shed for about 2 days before symptoms and in the early symptomatic phase, so people spread it without knowing.

## Must-know facts
- Symptoms: low-grade fever, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, sneezing, watery eyes, scratchy sore throat, bad breath, malaise, chills, headache, muscle aches.
- No cure: care is symptomatic.
- Allergic rhinitis differs: itching of nose, palate, throat, eyes and ears with sneezing, but no fever, and it is tied to pollen season (seasonal) or all year (perennial).

## Assessment
- Temperature, nasal discharge, throat, lung sounds, hydration.
- Look for signs that it has gone beyond a cold: high fever, chest pain, ear pain, difficulty swallowing.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Rest and plenty of fluids.
2. Prevent chilling.
3. Warm salt-water gargles for sore throat.
4. Steam or warm humidified air inhalation.
5. Handwashing and covering coughs to stop spread (infection control).

## Treatment and medications
- NSAIDs for aches; antihistamines for sneezing, runny nose and congestion (allergic rhinitis also uses nasal corticosteroid sprays and desensitization).
- Antibiotics do not treat viral colds (standard teaching; not in handout).

## Complications and red flags
- Sinus or ear infection, bronchitis, pneumonia in the vulnerable.

## Client teaching
- Blow the nose before using nasal medicine so it reaches the lining.
- Avoid allergens in allergic rhinitis.

## How the exam asks about it
- Which instruction is best: fluids, rest, handwashing and symptom relief.

## Related topics
[[Rhinitis: Allergic and Viral]], [[Pharyngitis: Acute and Chronic]], [[Stop Smoking and Tobacco Cessation]]

title: Respiratory Diagnostic Tests: Which Test for Which Disorder
body:
## What it is
A quick map from lung disease to the test the handout names.

## Must-know facts
- Spirometry: measures airflow obstruction in COPD.
- ABG: COPD (low PaO2 and pH, high CO2); ARDS (hypoxemia despite more oxygen); PE (hypoxemia and low CO2).
- Chest X-ray: COPD late (hyperinflation, flat diaphragm, bullae); pneumonia (consolidation); TB (presence and extent); pleurisy; PE (infiltrates, atelectasis, raised diaphragm on affected side); ARDS (bilateral infiltrates).
- CT scan: bronchiectasis (dilated bronchi); empyema; pleural effusion; laryngeal cancer work-up.
- Lateral decubitus X-ray: pleural effusion.
- Alpha-1-antitrypsin assay: inherited emphysema.
- Sputum Gram stain and culture/sensitivity: pneumonia and bronchiectasis; sputum smear/culture confirms TB.
- Tuberculin skin test (PPD, Mantoux): TB infection.
- Blood culture: bacteremia with pneumonia.
- V/Q scan, pulmonary angiography (best method), spiral CT: pulmonary embolism.
- Thoracentesis, pleural biopsy: pleural disease.
- Direct laryngoscopy, virtual endoscopy, optical imaging, CT/MRI: laryngeal cancer.
- BNP, echocardiogram, pulmonary artery catheter: help separate ARDS from cardiac causes.

## Assessment
- Check the order, consent, allergies and how the client must prepare.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Explain the test and obtain the specimen correctly (sputum: early morning, deep cough, before antibiotics is standard teaching).
2. After thoracentesis or bronchoscopy, watch breathing and oxygen saturation.
3. Label and send specimens promptly.

## How the exam asks about it
- Best test for PE: pulmonary angiography. Test to confirm TB: sputum smear/culture. Test for airflow limitation: spirometry. Imaging for bronchiectasis: CT.

## Related topics
[[COPD Management and Nursing Care]], [[Arterial Blood Gas Basics]], [[Chest X-ray and Pulse Oximetry]], [[Pulmonary Embolism]], [[Pulmonary Tuberculosis: Diagnosis and Classification]]

## Check against your textbook
- Specimen collection details are standard teaching, not from the handout.

title: Pleural and Chest Cavity Problems Compared
body:
## What it is
Six conditions put something abnormal in or around the pleural space. The content decides the name.

## Must-know facts
- Pneumothorax: air. Hyperresonance, diminished breath sounds, reduced chest movement; tension type shifts the trachea away.
- Pleural effusion: fluid (transudate or exudate), from heart failure, infection or nephrotic syndrome. Dyspnea, cannot lie flat, cough, pleuritic pain.
- Hemothorax: blood, from trauma. Possible shock, hidden blood loss.
- Empyema: pus, from pneumonia, abscess or chest trauma. Acutely ill client.
- Pleurisy: inflamed pleural layers rubbing; friction rub, sharp pain.
- Drainage rules: thoracentesis for effusion; chest tube plus water seal for pneumothorax and hemothorax; tube thoracostomy for loculated effusion or empyema; open thoracotomy drainage for thick pus.

## Assessment
- Breath sounds, percussion, tracheal position, pain pattern, chest X-ray.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Airway, breathing, oxygen; treat tension pneumothorax or shock immediately (life-threatening first).
2. Position upright if able; keep the chest drainage system sealed, below chest level, and patent.
3. Measure drainage; report sudden large blood output.
4. Splint the chest for coughing and give pain relief as ordered.

## How the exam asks about it
- Air = pneumothorax; fluid = effusion; blood = hemothorax; pus = empyema. A tension pneumothorax needs immediate decompression.

## How to reason about it
The most dangerous finding is the one that shifts the trachea or drops the blood pressure. Treat that before comfort measures.

## Related topics
[[Pneumothorax: Types and Findings]], [[Pleural Effusion]], [[Hemothorax]], [[Empyema Thoracis]], [[Pleurisy (Pleuritis)]], [[Pneumothorax: Management and Chest Tube Care]]

title: Heart Failure: Nursing Diagnoses and Care Priorities
body:
## What it is
A practical care plan for the client with heart failure (HF), built from the handout's nursing diagnoses and interventions.

## Must-know facts
- Handout nursing diagnoses: impaired gas exchange (ventilation-perfusion imbalance); decreased cardiac output (altered contractility, preload, afterload); activity intolerance (oxygen supply below demand); risk for pulmonary edema, pneumonia and dysrhythmias.
- Stages (ACC/AHA): A = at risk, no disease or symptoms; B = structural disease or left ventricular dysfunction, no symptoms; C = structural disease with current or past symptoms; D = refractory end-stage needing special care.
- Compensation: sympathetic stimulation (faster rate, vasoconstriction, more afterload) and renin-angiotensin activation (angiotensin II vasoconstriction; aldosterone causes sodium and water retention) lead to fluid overload.
- Left HF = lung signs (dyspnea, crackles, orthopnea, pink frothy sputum, S3). Right HF = body signs (neck vein distention, edema, hepatomegaly, ascites, weight gain).

## Assessment
- Breath sounds, rate, oxygen saturation, heart sounds, JVD, edema, liver size, abdominal girth, daily weight, intake and output.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Support breathing: semi-Fowler's or sitting up, oxygen as ordered (airway and breathing first).
2. Monitor vital signs, rhythm with a cardiac monitor, and changes.
3. Weigh daily at the same time; record intake and output (fluid overload check).
4. Give diuretics, ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, digoxin and vasodilators as prescribed; monitor potassium with diuretics.
5. Avoid unnecessary IV fluids.
6. Space activity with rest to match oxygen supply.
7. Assess dependent edema, including sacrum and thighs in bed-bound clients.

## Treatment and medications
- Diuretics reduce volume; ACE inhibitors lower afterload; beta-blockers raise ejection fraction and reduce ventricle size; digoxin strengthens contraction; vasodilators lower preload.

## Complications and red flags
- Pulmonary edema, dysrhythmias, worsening weight gain, drop in urine output.

## Client teaching
- Low-sodium diet; daily weight; report weight gain and worsening breathlessness; pace activity; sleep propped up.

## How the exam asks about it
- Which finding needs action first: rising dyspnea and crackles. Which teaching is best: daily weights and sodium limits.

## Related topics
[[Heart Failure: Types, Causes and Compensation]], [[Left-Sided versus Right-Sided Heart Failure]], [[Drugs Used in Heart Failure]], [[Acute Pulmonary Edema]]

title: COPD Types Compared: Blue Bloater and Pink Puffer
body:
## What it is
COPD is airflow limitation that is not fully reversible and usually worsens over time. It has two classic forms that appear in many exam questions.

## Must-know facts
- Chronic bronchitis ("blue bloater"): productive cough for at least 3 months a year for 2 years in a row; thick gelatinous sputum; wheezing and dyspnea later.
- Emphysema ("pink puffer"): destruction of alveolar walls; dyspnea, low exercise tolerance, minimal cough, barrel chest (raised anteroposterior diameter, flat diaphragm), weight loss.
- Panlobular emphysema: all air spaces enlarge; little inflammation; hyperinflated chest.
- Centrilobular emphysema: damage in the center of the lobule; chronic hypoxemia, hypercapnia, polycythemia, right-sided heart failure, central cyanosis, peripheral edema.
- Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency: inherited cause of emphysema.
- Tests: spirometry, ABG (low PaO2 and pH, high CO2), chest X-ray (hyperinflation, bullae).
- Treatment: smoking cessation, bronchodilators, corticosteroids, antibiotics and mucolytics; surgery includes bullectomy and lung volume reduction.

## Assessment
- Respiratory rate and pattern, breath sounds, oxygen saturation, weight, edema, sputum color.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Oxygen at low flow (1 to 2 L/min) as ordered: in COPD the drive to breathe can depend on low oxygen, so high flow risks respiratory depression (airway and breathing first, but safe dose).
2. Bronchodilators as prescribed; hydration to thin secretions.
3. Teach pursed-lip and diaphragmatic breathing; chest physiotherapy as ordered.
4. Small frequent meals and supplements to counter weight loss.
5. Alternate activity with rest; pulmonary rehabilitation.

## Complications and red flags
- Respiratory failure, right heart failure, recurrent infection; increased confusion or sleepiness signals rising CO2.

## Client teaching
- Stop smoking, avoid bronchial irritants, plan rests, recognize early infection.

## How the exam asks about it
- Barrel chest and thin = pink puffer (emphysema). Cyanotic, productive cough, edema = blue bloater (bronchitis). Oxygen flow for COPD: low.

## Related topics
[[COPD: Chronic Bronchitis and Emphysema]], [[COPD Management and Nursing Care]], [[Respiratory Acidosis]], [[Oxygen Therapy: Safety and Delivery Devices]]

## Check against your textbook
- The handout places centrilobular and panlobular features loosely; confirm which type causes which signs. The explanation for low-flow oxygen is standard teaching, not handout text.

title: Peripheral Vascular Disorders Compared: Buerger, Raynaud, DVT, Aneurysm
body:
## What it is
Four vessel problems that students confuse. Sort them by who gets them, what the color or pain does, and what is the main teaching.

## Must-know facts
- Buerger's disease: men 20 to 35, heavy smoking or chewing tobacco; small and medium arteries and veins inflamed. Foot cramps in the arch after exercise relieved by rest, rubor of the foot, absent pedal pulse. Stop all nicotine.
- Raynaud's phenomenon: women 16 to 40, cold climates; episodic color change white, blue, red; bilateral, symmetric. Avoid cold and nicotine; calcium channel blockers.
- Deep vein thrombosis: Virchow's triad (vessel injury, stasis, altered clotting). Swelling, heaviness, limb pain. Anticoagulants, compression stockings, elevate, walk.
- Aneurysm: localized dilation at a weak arterial wall. True, false, fusiform, saccular, dissecting. Control BP; surgery or endovascular graft; watch for rupture.

## Assessment
- Color, temperature, pulses, edema, pain pattern, skin integrity in both limbs.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Protect circulation: keep warm, avoid tight clothing and crossing legs.
2. For DVT, do not massage the leg (risk of embolism: standard teaching) and report chest pain or dyspnea at once (possible PE).
3. For suspected aneurysm rupture, treat sudden severe pain or falling BP as an emergency.
4. Teach stopping nicotine for Buerger's and Raynaud's.

## Complications and red flags
- Gangrene (Buerger's), pulmonary embolism (DVT), rupture (aneurysm).

## How the exam asks about it
- White-blue-red = Raynaud's. Young male smoker with absent pedal pulse = Buerger's. Unilateral leg swelling = DVT. Pulsating mass or sudden tearing pain = aneurysm.

## Related topics
[[Buerger's Disease (Thromboangiitis Obliterans)]], [[Raynaud's Phenomenon]], [[Deep Vein Thrombosis]], [[Aneurysms]], [[Pulmonary Embolism]]

## Check against your textbook
- The no-massage rule is standard teaching, not in the handout.
